clue.text: City mostly welcoming to English -—- until now!

indicators.note: a host welcoming a guest takes it in, so the shortened city name holds the next word inside it
mostly means not quite all, so the city's final letter is dropped

parts.note: Hereford is an English cathedral city

explanation.surface: A city that largely welcomes the English has, it seems, done so up to the present.
explanation.walkthrough: Hereford is a cathedral city in western England; the dash and exclamation make the definition look like an afterthought.
explanation.definitionFit: Heretofore is a formal adverb meaning before this time, synonymous with hitherto.

clue.text: Publican's spirit that's no good

indicators.note: that's no means without, so the good letter is removed

parts.note: a ghost is a spirit

explanation.surface: A pub landlord's drink is not up to scratch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spirit' suggests the pub's drink but means a ghost; dropping G leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A host is a landlord who receives guests, as a publican does in a pub.

clue.text: Philosophy getting Lear into a mess

indicators.note: a mess is a jumble, so these letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A philosophy gets King Lear into a muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into a' looks like a link but its letters join LEAR to form the anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A rationale is the underlying reasoning or set of principles behind something.

clue.text: He may fix problem with horn, securing hard cash first

indicators.note: securing means holding fast inside, so the horn word encloses the others

parts.note: a tooter is a horn that toots

indicators.note: first says the cash word comes before the letter for hard

parts.note: roubles are Russian currency
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A repairman will mend a broken horn, but wants cash up front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'problem with horn' reads as one idea, but 'problem' belongs to the definition; 'first' puts the cash before the hard letter, and roubles are hardly a hard currency.
explanation.definitionFit: A troubleshooter is someone employed to find and resolve faults or difficulties.

clue.text: Like ground meal, we're told? Fancy!

indicators.note: we're told signals that the answer is heard rather than seen

parts.note: flour is ground grain, so like ground meal is floury

explanation.surface: Is something said to resemble meal? How odd!
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sounds like FLOURY.
explanation.definitionFit: Fancy as an adjective means ornate, and flowery language is elaborately ornamented.

clue.text: Where one may spout rubbish about son's spirit

indicators.note: about means going round, so the rubbish word encloses the son letter

parts.note: rot means nonsense or rubbish
S is the abbreviation for son
rum is a spirit

explanation.surface: Someone spouting nonsense about a son's drinking habits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spout' suggests a fountain or whale, but here it means to speechify from a platform.
explanation.definitionFit: A rostrum is a raised platform from which a speaker addresses an audience.

clue.text: On which a boxer may be chief performer

definitions.text: On which a boxer may be
definitions.meaning: a boxer dog is walked on a leash
the star role in a play or film

explanation.walkthrough: The boxer is the dog breed, not a fighter in the ring.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog's leash is called a lead in Britain, and the star part in a show is the lead role.

clue.text: One of two writers turning material over

indicators.note: turning, read with the following over, means the fabric word is flipped end to end

parts.note: toile is a linen fabric; over completes the phrase turning over

explanation.surface: An author leafs through his material.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning ... over' is one indicator split around the fodder; George Eliot and T S Eliot are the two writers.
explanation.definitionFit: George Eliot the novelist and T S Eliot the poet both bore this surname.

clue.text: Facts about monarch receiving team? They're what's wanted

indicators.note: about means wrapped round, so the facts word encloses the rest

parts.note: data are facts

indicators.note: receiving means taking in, so the monarch holds the team

parts.note: ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen
a side is a team

explanation.surface: Facts about the Queen hosting a team are what everyone wants.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark separates the wordplay from the definition, which is the Latin plural for things wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Desiderata is Latin for things desired or needed, a plural noun.

clue.text: Flying officer 'S'? He's superior in rank

definitions.text: Flying officer 'S'? He's superior in rank

parts.words: Flying officer 'S'? He's superior in rank
parts.note: the letter S heads the word squadron, and this RAF officer outranks a flying officer

explanation.walkthrough: Flying Officer is itself an RAF rank below the answer, so the clue plays on both senses.
explanation.definitionFit: An RAF officer rank above flight lieutenant, commanding a flying unit.

clue.text: Spat excessively on radio receiver to begin with

indicators.note: to begin with says the receiver's word stands at the front of the answer

parts.note: a radio or television receiver is a set

indicators.note: words heard on radio are only heard, so the word for excessively is taken by its sound

parts.note: too means excessively, as in too hot

explanation.surface: Someone spat too much on a radio set at the start of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'radio receiver' looks like one phrase but splits: 'on radio' signals a word heard, and 'receiver' alone is the set.
explanation.definitionFit: A set-to is a brief fight or quarrel, the same as a spat.

clue.text: Old boy in Paris who sees about funeral rites

parts.note: OB is the abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil of a school

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for sees wraps round the French word

parts.note: taken as written
qui is French for who, French being the language of Paris

explanation.surface: A former pupil in Paris looks into arrangements for a burial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in Paris' tells the solver to use French; OB, for a former pupil, is common in British school slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Obsequies is a formal word for the ceremonies of a burial.

clue.text: Lookalike with money set out in this sort of jacket

parts.note: a double is a person who looks just like another

indicators.note: set out suggests things being arranged afresh, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: bread is slang for money
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lookalike carrying money is arranged in a particular jacket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges BREAD plus SET into BREASTED; 'set out' reads as one phrase but 'set' is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A double-breasted jacket has overlapping front panels with two rows of buttons, a style of coat.

clue.text: Feeble chap put up by doctor breaking foot

indicators.note: put up in a down clue means the word for chap is read upwards, backwards

parts.note: a man is a chap
taken as written

indicators.note: breaking means splitting apart, so the doctor letters go inside

parts.note: to foot a bill is to pay it
MB is a medical degree, Bachelor of Medicine

explanation.surface: A weak man is put up by a doctor who sets his broken foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up' suits a down clue, where reading backwards means reading upwards; 'foot' is the verb, as in footing a bill.
explanation.definitionFit: Namby-pamby means weak, ineffectual and sentimental.

clue.text: This writer's associated with a rebel school

parts.note: Jack Cade led a rebellion in Kent in 1450
the setter referring to himself: this writer's means my

explanation.surface: The setter boasts of a link with a school for rebels.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Cade led a famous English peasants' revolt in 1450; 'This writer's' comes last in the answer though it opens the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: An academy is a school or place of learning, especially a specialised one.

clue.text: Person demonstrating energy in springtime run

indicators.note: in places the energy symbol inside the month and run letters

parts.note: March is a month of spring
R is the cricket abbreviation for a run
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Someone protesting energetically on a spring jog.
explanation.walkthrough: E goes between MARCH and R.
explanation.definitionFit: A marcher is a protester walking in a demonstration.

clue.text: Stop one at a time, heading off with hesitation

parts.note: to halt is to stop

indicators.note: heading off means the first letter is removed

parts.note: singly means one at a time

explanation.surface: Stop people one by one and lead them away hesitantly.
explanation.walkthrough: SINGLY loses its S to give INGLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Haltingly means in a faltering, hesitant manner.

clue.text: Tree planted by American conductor

parts.note: the beech is a tree

explanation.surface: A tree has been planted by someone from America.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Thomas Beecham was a famous British conductor; 'planted by' just joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Thomas Beecham was a celebrated English orchestral conductor, founder of the Royal Philharmonic.

clue.text: Female European at centre of dancing

parts.note: May is a woman's name
a Pole is a European

explanation.surface: A woman from Europe is the focus of a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'centre of dancing' looks like a letter-picking instruction but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A maypole is the decorated post around which May Day dances are performed.

clue.text: Get in touch with permit to make lock

parts.note: to ring is to telephone, getting in touch
to let is to permit

explanation.surface: Phone someone to get permission for fitting a lock.
explanation.definitionFit: A ringlet is a curl of hair, and a lock is a tress of hair.

clue.text: Viscous substance upset on youngster's dress fabric

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means turned upside down, so the word reads backwards

parts.note: tar is a thick sticky substance
a teen is a youngster

explanation.surface: Sticky stuff has been spilt on a teenager's dress.
explanation.walkthrough: TAR upwards gives RAT, then TEEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Ratteen is a coarse twilled woollen cloth once used for clothing.

clue.text: This posy's on the ground — it requires chlorophyll

indicators.note: ground means crushed and broken up, so these letters are reworked

parts.note: the letters of posy's taken with the s

explanation.surface: A small bouquet lies on the floor, and plants need their green pigment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ground' looks like the floor but is the past tense of grind, the anagram signal for THIS POSYS ON THE.
explanation.definitionFit: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use the pigment to turn light into food.

clue.text: Instruct bachelor to get out of bed

indicators.note: to get out of means to leave, so the bachelor letter is removed

parts.note: a border is a flower bed along a garden edge

explanation.surface: Tell a single man to get up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bed' is a garden border, not a place to sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: To order is to instruct or command.

clue.text: Bouncer is ruddy short

indicators.note: short means the word is cut off before its end

parts.note: ruddy and bally are mild British euphemisms for bloody

explanation.surface: A nightclub doorman is extremely small.
explanation.walkthrough: BALLY loses its last letter. 'Bouncer' looks like a doorman but is anything that bounces.
explanation.definitionFit: A ball is something that bounces, so it can be called a bouncer.

clue.text: Created opening around front of reef (coral)

indicators.note: around means the first word goes round the reef's front letter

parts.note: made means created

indicators.note: front of picks the first letter of the following word

parts.note: a pore is a tiny opening, as in the skin

explanation.surface: Something formed an opening around the edge of a coral reef.
explanation.walkthrough: The brackets round 'coral' make it look like an aside, yet it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Madrepore is a stony reef-building coral.

clue.text: Go mad, struggling in teaching

indicators.note: struggling suggests writhing about, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone is going crazy trying to cope with teaching.
explanation.definitionFit: Dogma is a doctrine or body of beliefs taught as authoritative.

clue.text: Time to return, disturbed by queen's mews

indicators.note: disturbed by means broken into, so the queen's letter goes inside
to return says the word for time is read backwards

parts.note: a day is a period of time
R stands for Regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: It's time to go back, interrupted by the noise of the queen's cats.
explanation.walkthrough: DAY backwards is YAD, with R inside: YA-R-D. 'mews' looks like cat noises but is a row of stables.
explanation.definitionFit: A mews is a yard or courtyard of former stables in a city.

clue.text: Mint coin —— sovereign, possibly

parts.note: a penny is a coin
a sovereign, a monarch, is an example of a royal

explanation.surface: A mint issues coins, perhaps a gold sovereign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mint' looks like the place coins are made but is the herb.
explanation.definitionFit: Pennyroyal is a kind of mint plant, used as a herb.
